summary: Return all nodes at distance k from a target node in a binary tree.
mainInsight: A tree node only knows its children, so first record each node's parent (DFS). Then run BFS from the target over three neighbours (left, right, parent) with a visited set, stopping at depth k and returning that frontier.

approaches.name: Recursive distance bookkeeping
approaches.summary: Return distance to the target up the recursion and search the other side.

approaches.name: Parent map + BFS
approaches.summary: Treat the tree as an undirected graph.

commonMistakes: Searching only downwards from the target
Using node values (not identity) as keys when values repeat
edgeCases: k larger than the tree depth (empty result)

cards.answer: Record each node's parent, then BFS from the target over left, right and parent neighbours up to depth k. Clue: Distance is counted in edges in any direction, including upwards, but tree nodes only point down, so add parent links and search outwards from the target level by level.
keyPoints: Distance is counted in edges in any direction, including upwards, but tree nodes only point down, so add parent links and search outwards from the target level by level.
cards.explanation: With parent pointers the tree becomes an undirected graph, and BFS levels are exactly the distances from the target.

cards.answer: Nodes at distance k may lie above the target, via ancestors
cards.explanation: BFS from the target in all three directions.

promptVariants: Why is a visited set required in the BFS?
cards.answer: With parent edges, a node's neighbours include its parent and the parent's neighbours include the node, so without a visited set the BFS would bounce back and forth between them and revisit nodes (never stopping at the right depth).
keyPoints: Parent edges make cycles in the neighbour graph
cards.explanation: Equivalent to BFS on an undirected graph.
